name: Hereditary Alpha-Tryptasemia

prevalence.estimate: 4-6% of the general population carry extra TPSAB1 copies
prevalence.range: 3-6% prevalence of at least one extra copy

criteria.description: Elevated baseline serum tryptase (typically >8 ng/mL, often >11.4 ng/mL) on at least two occasions
Increased TPSAB1 gene copy number confirmed by droplet digital PCR or equivalent assay
Autosomal dominant inheritance pattern (first-degree relatives may also have elevated tryptase)
Exclusion of systemic mastocytosis and other clonal mast cell disorders

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Elevated baseline serum tryptase confirmed by genetic testing showing increased TPSAB1 copy number, with exclusion of clonal mast cell disease
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Many carriers are asymptomatic. Symptoms, when present, may overlap with MCAS and are thought to be modified by the gene dosage (more copies = higher tryptase and potentially more symptoms). HaT can coexist with and worsen other mast cell disorders.

common.notes: By definition; this is the biochemical hallmark, though not strictly a symptom

common.symptomName: Chronic GI symptoms (bloating, abdominal pain, IBS-like)

occasional.notes: Connective tissue features overlap with EDS phenotype
Risk increased when combined with other mast cell disorders

laboratory: Baseline serum tryptase elevated (typically >8 ng/mL; increases ~2.5 ng/mL per extra TPSAB1 copy)
Total and mature tryptase ratio may be altered
Normal CBC and other routine labs
genetic: Increased copy number of TPSAB1 gene (encoding alpha-tryptase) on chromosome 16p13.3
Detected by droplet digital PCR (ddPCR) targeting TPSAB1
Autosomal dominant inheritance with variable expressivity
Gene dosage effect: more copies correlate with higher tryptase levels
other: Bone marrow biopsy: normal (no mast cell aggregates, no KIT D816V, no aberrant CD25) - important to distinguish from mastocytosis
Family screening: first-degree relatives often have elevated tryptase

distinguishingFeatures: SM has KIT D816V mutation and abnormal mast cell aggregates on bone marrow
HaT has elevated tryptase from gene duplication, not clonal mast cells
MCAS has episodic mediator release symptoms with acute tryptase rise
HaT has constitutively elevated baseline tryptase
HaT may predispose to or coexist with MCAS
CKD can elevate tryptase due to reduced clearance
HaT has normal renal function with genetic confirmation

redFlags: Baseline tryptase >20 ng/mL (even with HaT confirmed, should exclude coexisting mastocytosis)
Severe or recurrent anaphylaxis (HaT may amplify risk in context of other mast cell disease)
Onset of new B-symptoms or organomegaly (consider hematologic neoplasm)
references: Lyons JJ, et al. Elevated basal serum tryptase identifies a multisystem disorder associated with increased TPSAB1 copy number. Nat Genet. 2016;48(12):1564-1569.
Lyons JJ. Hereditary alpha tryptasemia: genotyping and associated clinical features. Immunol Allergy Clin North Am. 2018;38(3):483-495.
Greiner G, et al. Hereditary alpha tryptasemia is a valid genetic biomarker for severe mediator-related symptoms in mastocytosis. Blood. 2021;137(2):238-247.
